stops.name: Sainte-Catherine-de-Fierbois, the sword left behind the altar
stops.campa: Riding south of Tours, Charles stops at the wayside shrine of Saint Catherine at Fierbois, the tradition holds he founded it, and leaves there a sword marked with five crosses, an offering for the victory, laid up behind the altar for the hand God will one day choose. There it sinks into the earth and the rust of seven hundred years. In 1429 a girl from Domremy, who has never seen it, will send for it by name and place, and the rust will fall away at a touch. The Hammer's road and the Maid's road cross here, at a village altar, across seven centuries.
stops.quote: When I was at Tours or at Chinon, I sent to seek a sword which was in the church of Saint Catherine of Fierbois, behind the altar; and it was found there at once, all covered with rust.
stops.quote_source: Testimony of Jeanne d'Arc, Trial of Condemnation, 27 February 1431

stops.name: Lyon, Burgundy taken in hand
stops.campa: The year after the great battle Charles descends the Saône to Lyon and takes Burgundy in hand, setting his own judges and faithful men over the region as far as Marseille's hinterland. The southern magnates, Roman in their letters and Gothic in their pride, discover what the Saxons learned: the mayor's writ now runs wherever his horses can water. It is administration carried like a campaign: lists, oaths, hostages, the quiet half of the hammer's work.

stops.name: The mouth of the Boarn, Frisia: the temples of the sea-god broken
stops.campa: Charles builds a fleet, the Hammer goes to sea, and sails into the heart of free Frisia, to the mouth of the Boarn. King Poppo brings his boats and his host; the battle goes to the Franks and Poppo is slain. Then Charles breaks the sanctuaries of the heathen gods, the temples of the sea-god among the terpen, and burns them, and carries great spoil home. Where Radbod once drew his foot from the font, the font now comes to Frisia behind the ships.

stops.name: Blaye on the Gironde: the death of Eudo, Aquitaine entered
stops.campa: Duke Eudo dies, and Charles crosses the Loire at once, takes Bordeaux and the fortress of Blaye above the Gironde, and receives the submission of the Aquitanians. He allows Eudo's son Hunald the duchy: on oath, as a grant held of his hand, the new grammar of holding. The old free south learns the case-endings of vassalage. On this rock over the brown water, later ages will say Roland lies buried; the roads of the epics are already being surveyed.

stops.name: Orléans, the church lands and the canon's grumble
stops.campa: War on every frontier is paid for in land, and Charles takes it where it lies richest: from the Church. Bishop Eucherius of Orléans, who objects, is removed into exile; abbeys and sees are handed to fighting men who owe horses and mail for them: the first knight-fiefs, the seed of a whole world. The canon grumbles and remembers: a holy man is later shown Charles in torment for the plunder of the saints, and his opened tomb at Saint-Denis yields a fleeing dragon and a vault blackened as by fire. Both truths hold: the realm saved, the price entered in heaven's ledger.

stops.name: Avignon, stormed like Jericho
stops.campa: Avignon on its rock has been handed to the Saracens by Maurontus, duke of Provence, and garrisoned against the Franks. Charles sends his brother Childebrand ahead, comes up with the host, and takes the city by storm. The chronicle reaches for Scripture to say how: as at Jericho, with a great shout and the blare of trumpets, over the walls on ropes and engines. The city burns. The Rhone is a Frankish river again, and the army turns down it toward the sea.
stops.quote: In the manner of Jericho, with a great shout and the sound of trumpets, with battering rams and rope ladders they rushed over walls and buildings, and took that fortified city and burned it.

stops.name: Narbonne, the siege on the Aude
stops.campa: Charles crosses into Gothic Septimania and sits down before Narbonne, the Saracen capital north of the Pyrenees, ringing it with lines along the Aude and blockading its garrison under Yusuf. The city that Rome called Narbo Martius holds its walls; the Hammer, who has taken every city he ever touched, cannot starve this one before relief comes by sea. Narbonne will wait twenty-two years for his son. Even in the canon of a saved Europe, one gate stays shut.

stops.name: The river Berre, by the lagoons of Sigean
stops.campa: A relieving army lands from Spain under Omar ibn Chaled and marches for Narbonne. Charles leaves his siege lines and meets it in the valley of the Berre, where the river crawls to the salt lagoons. The Franks break the host; its general falls; the survivors are driven into the marshes and the étang, where men in mail drown among the reeds and the salt-pans, and boats hunt the swimmers. The lagoon country south of Narbonne becomes the canon's image of the sea taking back the invasion.

stops.name: Nîmes, fire in the arena
stops.campa: Marching home, Charles makes Septimania untenable behind him: he wrecks what a garrison could hold. At Nîmes he sets fire to the gates of the Roman amphitheatre, the thousand-year oval the Goths and Saracens had made a fortress; the smoke-blackening on the stones is shown for centuries after. The chronicle lists the ruined towns like hammer-strokes: the method is scorched earth pronounced with Latin precision.

stops.name: Béziers and Agde, the walls thrown down
stops.campa: Béziers on its hill and Agde the black basalt port are taken, their walls and citadels demolished, their suburbs burned; Maguelone is razed on its island. No strongpoint is left standing between the Rhone and the lines of Narbonne that a returning fleet could garrison against him. The Hammer's mercy is architectural: he does not massacre these towns, he simply unbuilds them. Behind the army, the coast road smokes from the Rhone to the Pyrenees.

stops.name: Chelles, the empty throne
stops.campa: King Theuderic IV, the boy Charles once fetched from the cloister of Chelles, dies, and Charles raises no successor. The throne of Clovis simply stands empty, and the realm does not fall; the charters begin to be dated by the years of an absent king, and then by the years of Charles himself. It is the boldest act of his life performed as an omission. A kingdom discovers it has been governed by its mayor so long that the crown has become furniture.

stops.name: Marseille and the sea-rocks of Maurontus
stops.campa: Provence rises once more under Duke Maurontus, and Charles comes down the Rhone a second time with Childebrand, and with Lombard king Liutprand as sworn ally at his back. Marseille is taken; the rebellion dissolves; Maurontus flees to a fortress on inaccessible rocks above the sea, and the canon leaves him there, clinging to the last vertical yard of independent Gaul. From the Alps to the two seas, every duke, bishop, and city now holds of the Hammer's hand.
